newsitem.title: USA: TWA 800 probe not ready to blame mechanical fault. [CORRECTED 21:05 GMT]
newsitem.headline: TWA 800 probe not ready to blame mechanical fault. [CORRECTED 21:05 GMT]

text.p: There was no evidence that a criminal act brought down TWA flight 800 last summer although investigators are still not ready to declare that it was a mechanical problem that sparked the fuel tank explosion.

"All of our efforts to date have failed to uncover any credible evidence that the loss of Flight 800 was the result of a criminal act," Federal Bureau of Investigation official James Kallstrom told a House Transportation subcommittee Thursday.

"There is no evidence of a bomb or a missile impact in the wreckage," National Transportation Safety Board Chairman (corrects from "National Transportation Board Chairman") James Hall told the same panel.
On July 17, 1996, the TWA Boeing 747 exploded over the Atlantic Ocean near Long Island on its way from New York to Paris. All 230 people aboard were killed.
Investigators are united in blaming the explosion of fuel fumes and air in the plane's centre fuel tank for the destruction of the jet but what touched it off is in doubt.

Kallstrom and Hall, in answer to lawmakers' questions, were careful not to rule out that perhaps a small explosive charge could have set off the blast despite the appearance that the evidence now points to a mechanical cause.
Hall said it could be another year before the investigation into the crash of TWA Flight 800 was completed, but he was optimistic that the accident would be resolved.
"I think we will be able to solve this mystery Mr. Chairman," he said. "I would hope we could have this completed by the second anniversary of this accident..."
Kallstrom said the FBI had not reached the end of its investigation but said his organisation was close to conclusion.

"Barring some new disclosure or information, we are now in the final phase of our investigation," he said, adding later that the FBI might be only 60 to 90 days away from declaring whether a criminal act was involved.
In anticipation of the FBI ruling, and completion of a large number of its own tests, the NTSB is planning a public hearing into the crash for December in Baltimore, Hall said.

Hall said his investigators were pursuing a number of theories on how the centre fuel tank ignited, including overheating of the tank's scavenge pump, static electricity, a short circuit in a fuel probe and degrading of wires passing through the tank.
Also being pursued, Hall said, was the possibility of a small explosive charge and the possibility of a high speed particle such as a fragment from a meteorite, space debris or a missile warhead.
In late July and early August the NTSB will set off small explosive charges around a centre wing tank of a retired Boeing 747 in England as part of its continuing tests.
The board has also leased a Boeing 747 for flight tests this weekend to recreate as much as possible the fuel temperature conditions onboard TWA Flight 800.
Hall repeated his disappointment with the Federal Aviation Administration for failing to adopt interim measures to prevent similar explosions.

But FAA associate administrator Guy Gardner told the panel that its technical data did not show the effectiveness of the NTSB idea to add an amount of cooler fuel to the centre tank to minimise the danger of explosion.
A number of committee members called on the two agencies to cooperate more closely to resolve the issue.
"It seems the two agencies should not be having a hissy fit over this," said Representative James Oberstar, a Democrat from Minnesota.
